sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in a text extraction of the Louisiana copy (the extractor did not keep every table column, so placement was checked against the course's own reading of 2026-11-09 in ems-sources.ts). EMR: CPR and AED, tourniquet and wound packing, naloxone, oral airway, BVM, oxygen; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector, aspirin, oral glucose, CPAP, 12-lead acquisition (not interpretation), transport. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways and a limited list of IV and IM medications including dextrose and glucagon. Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, intubation and the wider formulary. No newer model was found 2026-11-11 (EMS.gov's page was unavailable; the only other 'update' found is the 2017 change notice adding tourniquets, wound packing and naloxone to EMR and EMT).

brief.situation: 07:42. You and your partner are EMRs on a fire engine, first on scene at a gym. A 58-year-old man collapsed on a treadmill about 90 seconds before you walked in; staff called 911 and stood back. He lies on his back on the floor.
handover: Dispatch sent a basic (BLS) ambulance, about 9 minutes out. Paramedics (ALS) come only if you ask for them.
Your partner carries the AED and the airway bag (oral airways, BVM). A staff member will help if you give clear jobs.
As an EMR you do not transport and do not interpret rhythms: the AED decides whether to shock.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Compressions run while 'Compressions: yes' shows. Checks, analysis and shocks need hands off the chest; every second off counts.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when the ambulance crew takes over, then a debrief scores what you did.

why.question: He was gasping when you arrived. What told you to start compressions, and why go straight back to compressions after a shock instead of checking for a pulse?

parts.label: Recognizing the arrest
parts.criteria: Unresponsive with no normal breathing (occasional gasps are agonal breathing, not breathing) and no definite pulse within a 10-second check means cardiac arrest: start compressions at once.
parts.modelAnswer: He did not respond, and the occasional snoring gasp is agonal breathing, a sign of cardiac arrest, not breathing. With no definite pulse in a check of 10 seconds or less, start compressions right away.

parts.label: After the shock
parts.criteria: Resume compressions immediately after a shock; a pulse, if one returns, is usually not palpable at once, and the AED reanalyzes after 2 minutes. Keep every pause short to keep the compression fraction high.
parts.modelAnswer: Right after a shock the heart rarely pumps well enough to feel a pulse, so a pulse check just adds hands-off time. Resume compressions immediately and let the AED reanalyze at 2 minutes; check for a pulse when it advises no shock.

noProgress.rationale: A shockable arrest handed over without a single shock lost the one treatment an EMR's AED offers; this case calls it harm.

expertPath.text: Scene safe, gloves. Tap and shout: no response, occasional gasps. Radio: confirmed arrest, send ALS.
Breathing and pulse check, under 10 s: no pulse, gasps only. Compressions at once; partner puts the AED pads on while you compress.
Clear for the analysis, shock, and back on the chest immediately. Partner: oral airway and BVM, 30:2.
Switch compressors at the 2-minute analysis. No shock advised: pulse check finds a pulse. Breath every 6 s; recheck every 2 min.
Hand over to the paramedics: times, one shock, pulse found, what he needs now.

asystole.headline: VF faded to a flat line
asystole.body: Fibrillation lasts only minutes without blood flow. Look at when compressions began (gasps are not breathing), when the AED went on, and how long hands were off the chest.

noShock.headline: No shock before the crew arrived
noShock.body: An EMR's most powerful tool is the AED. Pads go on while compressions continue, as soon as it is at hand; then clear, shock, and straight back to compressions.

roscHandoff.headline: Pulse back, clean handoff
roscHandoff.body: Fast recognition, compressions within seconds, an early shock, short pauses and a complete report. That is the chain of survival as an EMR runs it.

roscGaps.headline: Pulse back, with gaps
roscGaps.body: He has a pulse, but check your timeline: the start of compressions, the first shock, pauses after shocks and the report.

cprHandoff.headline: Handed over still in arrest
cprHandoff.body: The shock came too late or the pauses were too long for it to work. Every minute without flow costs viability; compress early, pad early, and keep pauses short.

time_up.headline: No handover
time_up.body: Fifteen minutes passed without a handover.

scoring.modelReasoning: Unresponsive with only occasional gasps is cardiac arrest until proven otherwise: agonal breathing is not breathing. Check breathing and pulse together in 10 seconds or less, start high-quality compressions (100-120/min, at least 2 inches, full recoil), and get the AED on while compressions continue. Clear for analysis, shock when advised, and resume compressions immediately: a pulse is rarely palpable right after a shock and the AED reanalyzes after 2 minutes. Switch compressors about every 2 minutes, ventilate 30:2 with an oral airway and BVM, ask for paramedics early, and hand over with times, shocks and current status.

gasps.explain: Occasional gasps in an unresponsive person are agonal breathing, part of cardiac arrest. Treat them as no breathing: compressions and the AED.
